text: Market access for a Preah Vihear smallholder means more than knowing a willing buyer — it also requires a practical way to move the product to that buyer while preserving quality and keeping the transaction profitable. This includes finding a realistic buyer (trader, collector, mill, processor, cooperative, or larger buyer), comparing the buyer's price against transport, loading, weighing, drying, grading, storage, and spoilage costs, and, for livestock, managing animal-health and transport risk. During the wet season (roughly May–October), muddy roads and difficult transport can make farm-gate collection more valuable even at a lower quoted price; during the dry season (roughly November–April), transport is often easier but heat, dust, and water shortages become the bigger constraint, particularly for perishable products. Small production volumes are a real limitation for many Preah Vihear smallholders, which is why aggregation with neighboring farmers or through a farmer group/cooperative can matter more than finding the single highest-priced buyer. Storable products (properly dried rice, cashew) offer more flexibility than highly perishable products (vegetables, milk, eggs), which depend on speed and proximity rather than storage. The core principle is that a buyer is not automatically "better" for offering a higher price — the right channel is whichever gives an acceptable net return with manageable risk, and the best channel can change between wet and dry season and between commodities.
